messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Police Officer
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Kwame is an 18-year-old African American man who recently began work as a police officer and came to treatment after months of feeling increasingly on edge in ways he no longer trusted himself to manage. When he speaks about what happened to him, he does not tell it as a smooth story. He returns instead to a handful of fixed images from childhood, each one sharp and separate, “like pictures” that arrive without warning. In one, he is very small and standing in a hallway outside the kitchen at night. In another, the house has gone unusually quiet in the strange way it did just before violence broke out. In another, he can see his mother’s posture change and his own body flattening, shoulders tightened, as if bracing before he even knew exactly what would happen next. He witnessed domestic violence repeatedly as a child, and what remains with him now is not only the visual memory of those moments but the felt sense of being trapped in the same position, unable to move, unable to stop what was happening.

When these memories come back, Kwame does not experience them as distant recollections. He feels his body take on that old stance, muscles tensing as if he is once again a child pinned to the spot outside the room. What comes with it most strongly is grief. He describes being overtaken by a heavy, painful sadness when he remembers those nights, not only fear but a sense of loss so strong it leaves him quiet for hours afterward. He has come to believe that something about the way he reacts means there is something wrong with him. He worries that these sudden bodily reactions and the force of the memories mean he is “going crazy.” Just as often, he concludes something harsher: that he cannot rely on himself. If he could not stop bad things then, he thinks, maybe he still cannot stop bad things now.

Those beliefs have settled into the way he moves through daily life. Since joining the police force, he has noticed how quickly he scans every setting for danger. Walking into a break room, a convenience store, or a family home on a call, his eyes immediately pick out anything that could be used as a weapon: a heavy stapler, a kitchen knife left near a sink, a glass bottle on a table, a metal tool by a doorway. He knows this fits his work in some ways, but he also feels how relentless it is, as if his attention cannot loosen even when the situation does not require it. People acting suspiciously are especially hard for him to tolerate. A pause too long before answering, someone shifting their hands out of sight, a glance exchanged across a room—these moments bring an immediate sense of threat. He feels uncomfortable quickly, in a full-body way, before he has had time to think.

Silence is particularly difficult. On patrol, if a house becomes suddenly quiet as he approaches, or if conversation inside stops for a beat, his stomach drops. What frightens him most is the sense that unusual silence means something dangerous is about to happen, the same charged stillness he remembers from childhood just before violence erupted. He avoids unfamiliar places whenever he can because not knowing the layout leaves him feeling exposed and unable to assess danger. Off duty, this has narrowed his life. He turns down invitations if he has not been to the restaurant, apartment, or neighborhood before. Friends have started to joke that he is hard to get out of the house, and he hears the distance growing even if he does not explain it.

Unexpected touch is another flashpoint. If a colleague comes up behind him and claps a hand on his shoulder, or someone brushes past him before he registers they are there, his whole body jolts. He hates the instant of being unprepared and then feels ashamed of how strong the reaction is. These moments feed his fear that he is losing control of himself. He does not experience himself as steady or dependable; he experiences himself as a person who should have learned by now how to handle things and somehow has not.

What finally brought Kwame in was not one dramatic incident but the accumulation of them. He had begun dreading ordinary parts of his shift, especially entering unfamiliar buildings or standing in sudden quiet. He was withdrawing more from friends, and after an unexpected touch at work left him visibly shaken, he could not dismiss it as just stress. In seeking help, he says he wants to understand why his body still reacts as though those childhood moments are happening now. What he fears most is that he will keep feeling helpless in the face of danger and that his reactions mean he is no longer in command of himself. What he hopes, more quietly, is that he might someday remember without feeling pinned back into the posture of that child in the hallway.
